title: The house filled with the odor (John 12:1–8)
hookLine: Mary of Bethany anoints his feet with costly nard

cards: A scent doesn't stay politely in one corner. It fills a room, gets into curtains, follows people home on their clothes. Long after the guests have gone, a house can still smell of the dinner.

Six days before the Passover, Jesus is back in Bethany at a dinner, and Lazarus, the man who was dead, is sitting at the table. Then his sister Mary opens a jar, and nobody in the house can miss what happens next.

teach.b: Martha is serving; Lazarus is at the table.

And Mary takes a pound of ointment, spikenard, of great price, John says. She pours it on Jesus's feet and wipes them with her hair. Then John adds one sentence that's pure memory, as if he can still smell it.
The Douay-Rheims says: "and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment." Odour is the British spelling of odor, and here it just means fragrance.
Judas objects: why wasn't this sold for three hundred pence and given to the poor?
A penny there is a denarius, roughly a day's pay for a laborer, so this jar is worth three hundred days of a laborer's pay, poured out in a minute.
John says plainly that Judas didn't care about the poor; he kept the purse and helped himself.
Jesus defends her: let her alone, she has kept it for the day of my burial.

teach.h: THE HOUSE FILLED WITH THE ODOR.
teach.b: Then: "For the poor you have always with you; but me you have not always." People sometimes hear that as a shrug about poverty.
Readers who know Deuteronomy hear an echo instead: the poor will not be wanting in the land, it says, and so open your hand to them. Read that way, Jesus is saying, this moment won't come again.
Mary seems to understand what the others don't: he is about to die. So she does something extravagant, physical and unforgettable.

how: The Church reads the anointing at Bethany at Mass on the Monday of Holy Week.

o: a costly perfume made from a plant
a cheap oil for burning in lamps
a spice baked into Passover bread

games.q: the dinner at Bethany — tap the pairs.

s: the poor you have always with you means poverty doesn't matter
readers hear an echo of Deuteronomy 15, which commands an open hand to the poor.
Judas priced the ointment at three hundred pence
in Matthew 20 a penny is a laborer's pay for a day.
John says Judas cared deeply about the poor
John says he kept the purse and helped himself.

games.q: you're at the dinner. Mary has just poured three hundred pence worth of perfume on Jesus's feet. Judas complains. what does Jesus say?
o: Judas is right; it should have been sold.
let her alone; she kept it for my burial.
next time, give half to the poor.
games.why: he defends her. she has done something for his burial, a moment that won't come again.

practice: Breathe slowly through your nose a few times and notice what you can smell right now, even faintly.
Then think of one person and one generous thing they would notice, flowers on a table, bread warming, a candle lit, a handwritten note, and let it become concrete in your mind.
If you pray, offer it the way Mary offered the jar; if not, just hold the person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Nard. The costly perfume Mary of Bethany poured on Jesus's feet, filling the whole house with its fragrance. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: nard, spikenard, the costly perfume in John 12:3.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole house knew. A gift poured out doesn't stay in its corner. See you tomorrow.
